prompt: A game console experiences improved frame rates because the compiler uses efficient memory-access techniques. Which architectural component is most directly involved?
explanation: Addressing modes are the ways an instruction may name its operand, and they are the part of the ISA a compiler actually chooses between when it optimises memory access.

why.a: Wrong. Control signals are generated by the hardware itself. A compiler cannot select them.
why.b: Wrong. Buses are physical organization. The compiler cannot choose a different bus.
why.c: Correct. The stem says the COMPILER did it, and addressing modes are the memory-access choice available to a compiler.
why.d: Wrong. Memory chips are hardware fitted to the board, invisible to and unselectable by the compiler.

prompt: Which of the following would most likely be visible to a programmer?
explanation: Instruction formats are part of the ISA, which is by definition the programmer-visible interface. Everything else listed sits below that line, in the organization.

why.a: Wrong. A program behaves the same whichever memory technology is fitted, so the technology is invisible to it.
why.b: Wrong. Cache is deliberately transparent: it changes timing, never results.
why.c: Wrong. Control circuitry is deep microarchitecture, generated inside the processor and never named by a program.
why.d: Correct. A programmer or compiler must know the exact bit layout to encode an instruction at all.

prompt: A programmer wants to know whether a processor supports floating-point instructions. This concern relates to:
explanation: Which instructions EXIST is an architecture question, settled by the ISA. How fast they run would be an organization question.

why.a: Wrong. Control signals implement instructions that already exist, they do not decide which exist.
why.b: Wrong. The memory hierarchy affects how quickly operands arrive, not whether an instruction is supported.
why.c: Wrong. Bus organization is about moving data between units, again a speed matter.
why.d: Correct. The set of supported instructions is exactly what the architecture defines.

prompt: A compiler attempts to minimize memory accesses by keeping frequently used variables inside processor registers. Which instruction category benefits the most?
explanation: Register-register arithmetic takes both operands from registers and writes the result back to a register, so it never touches memory at all.

why.a: Correct. Operands already in registers is precisely the condition this category needs.
why.b: Wrong. Privileged instructions are about protection and operating-system mode, not operand location.
why.c: Wrong. Input/output instructions talk to devices, so keeping variables in registers does not help them.
why.d: Wrong. Interrupt instructions handle external events. They are unaffected by where a variable lives.

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes ISA from microarchitecture?

options.text: ISA defines how instructions are executed internally.

explanation: The ISA is WHAT the machine does, the interface a programmer codes against. The microarchitecture is HOW it is done inside: transistors, caches, pipelines.

why.a: Wrong. Transistor layout is physical implementation, the far end of microarchitecture.
why.b: Wrong. Cache replacement, whether LRU or random, is invisible to a program and is a microarchitecture policy.
why.c: Correct, and this is the definition to memorise.
why.d: Wrong. "How instructions are executed internally" is the definition of MICROARCHITECTURE, offered here as the near miss.

prompt: Which instruction is typically executed immediately after a successful comparison operation?
explanation: A compare sets the condition flags. The instruction that reads those flags and decides where to go next is the conditional branch.

why.a: Wrong. Divide is arithmetic. It neither reads nor needs the condition flags.
why.b: Correct. Compare then branch is the standard pair, which is how an if statement is built.
why.c: Wrong. STORE writes a register to memory and ignores the flags.
why.d: Wrong. LOAD reads memory into a register and also ignores the flags.

prompt: Which instruction category is responsible for moving data between CPU registers and memory?
explanation: Data transfer is the category that only moves values around: LOAD, STORE, MOVE. It changes location, never value.

why.a: Wrong. Floating-point instructions compute on real numbers, they do not exist to move data.
why.b: Correct. LOAD, STORE and MOVE are its members.
why.c: Wrong. Control instructions change which instruction runs next, not where data sits.
why.d: Wrong. Logical instructions such as AND, OR and NOT compute on values already held.

prompt: Which instruction would most likely access the main memory?
explanation: LOAD fetches an operand from main memory into a register. The others work on values already held in registers.

why.a: Wrong. XOR is a logical operation between register values.
why.b: Correct. Reaching into memory for an operand is the entire job of a LOAD.
why.c: Wrong. SHIFT moves bits within a single register.
why.d: Wrong. ADD sums register values, which is why compilers work so hard to keep operands in registers.

prompt: Why are specialized instructions such as SIMD instructions introduced into modern processors?
explanation: SIMD is Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one instruction applies the same operation to many values at once, which is exactly what graphics and matrix work need.

why.a: Wrong, and nobody adds a feature to make fetching SLOWER.
why.b: Wrong. SIMD makes the datapath wider and the design more complex, not the cache simpler.
why.c: Wrong, and backwards. SIMD needs wide vector registers, so it adds register state rather than removing it.
why.d: Correct. One instruction, many data elements, which is where the name comes from.

prompt: A software developer successfully runs the same compiled application on two processors from different manufacturers. This is possible because both processors implement the same:
explanation: A compiled binary is a stream of ISA instructions. Any processor implementing that ISA can execute it, whoever built it and however differently it is built inside.

why.a: Correct. The ISA is the contract a binary is written against.
why.b: Wrong, and the point of the question is that the two microarchitectures are almost certainly different.
why.c: Wrong. Control unit design is internal and varies freely between manufacturers.
why.d: Wrong. Cache sizes and levels differ between vendors and are invisible to the binary anyway.

prompt: Which instruction category primarily changes the sequence of program execution?
explanation: Control transfer instructions, the jumps, branches, calls and returns, write a new value into the program counter and so redirect the flow.

why.a: Wrong. Arithmetic computes values, then execution simply falls through to the next instruction.
why.b: Correct. Jump, branch, call and return are its members.
why.c: Wrong. Data transfer moves values between registers and memory, leaving the flow untouched.
why.d: Wrong. Logical instructions compute a result. Only a following branch changes the sequence.

topic: What the ISA does not define
prompt: Which of the following is NOT defined by an Instruction Set Architecture?
explanation: The ISA defines the instructions, their formats, their addressing modes and the registers you can name. How the ALU is built to carry out an ADD is microarchitecture.

why.a: Correct, and remember the question asks which is NOT. Two chips with the same ISA may use completely different adder designs, and no program can tell.
why.b: Wrong choice. Addressing modes ARE in the ISA, since an instruction must state how it names its operand.
why.c: Wrong choice. Instruction formats ARE in the ISA, since the bit layout must be fixed for code to be encoded.
why.d: Wrong choice. Programmer-visible registers ARE in the ISA, since instructions name them directly.

prompt: A processor supports arithmetic, logical, branch, load/store, and input/output instructions. These collectively constitute its:
explanation: Every instruction a processor understands, taken together, is its instruction set. The five categories listed are the standard grouping of that set.

why.a: Correct. The word "collectively" is the clue: all the instructions together are the set.
why.b: Wrong. The address bus is a set of wires carrying a location, not a collection of instructions.
why.c: Wrong. The register file is storage inside the CPU, not the operations it can perform.
why.d: Wrong. Pipeline stages are how one instruction is processed in steps, unrelated to how many instructions exist.
